questions.prompt: A utility's messages are sent to a hosted model. For the same complaint, the provider reports 14 tokens for the English version and 46 for the Modern Standard Arabic version. The Arabic text has no diacritics and no typos. What is the most likely cause?
options: The Arabic text was not normalised before it was sent
The Arabic message contains more words than the English one
The model's tokeniser was trained mostly on English text
The provider counts Arabic characters instead of tokens
questions.explanation: A byte-level tokeniser with few Arabic merges falls back to short byte pieces, about two per letter, so the same content costs about three times the tokens.
misconceptions: Reaches for normalisation when the text is already clean
Counts words: Arabic versions of the same complaint have fewer words, not three times more
Confuses the unit: providers bill tokens, and characters would give a different ratio

questions.prompt: An Arabic WordPiece tokeniser turns the word العِداد (with one diacritic) into [UNK], and the same word without the diacritic into two known pieces. Where does the failure come from?
options: The vocabulary has no piece with a diacritic
The classifier after the tokeniser was never trained on this word
The message mixes two scripts in one word
The word is too long for the tokeniser's maximum length
questions.explanation: The tokeniser's training text had no diacritics, so no vocabulary piece contains one and the whole word becomes unknown.
misconceptions: Locates the failure after the step where it happens
Sees a script problem where there is one script
Blames length: the word has six letters

questions.prompt: A routing call sends 200 tokens of instructions and a message of 20 tokens. The input price is 0.50 USD per million tokens. What do 1,000 calls cost in input tokens?
options: 0.01 USD
0.10 USD
0.11 USD
1.10 USD
questions.explanation: Each call sends 220 tokens; 1,000 calls are 220,000 tokens, which is 0.22 of a million, times 0.50 USD = 0.11 USD.
misconceptions: Prices the messages only and forgets the instructions
Prices the instructions only and forgets the messages
Slips one decimal place in the conversion to millions

questions.prompt: You compute the attention weights of one head for a six-token sentence in a decoder. What must be true of the row of the third token?
options: It is zero for tokens one and two and sums to 1
It is equal for all six tokens and sums to the number of tokens
It is zero for the third token itself and sums to the number of heads
It is zero for tokens four to six and sums to 1
questions.explanation: A decoder masks every later position before the softmax, so those weights are exactly zero, and a softmax row sums to 1.
misconceptions: Reverses the mask: a decoder looks back, not ahead
Confuses attention with an average over all tokens
Mixes up the softmax over tokens with the number of heads

questions.prompt: A team must tag every word of a message as part of a district name, part of an account number, or neither. They have 3,000 labelled messages and need answers in milliseconds on a processor. Which design fits best?
options: A decoder prompted to rewrite the message with tags
An encoder with one classification score per token
An embedding model and a nearest-neighbour search per message
An encoder with one classification score per message
questions.explanation: The task needs one decision per token, with both sides of the word in view: an encoder with a token-classification head does that in one pass.
misconceptions: Generates text for a labelling task, at many times the latency
Returns similar messages, not a label for each word
Gives one label for the whole message, which cannot mark single words

questions.prompt: A search returns its top 10 messages for a query. The query has 6 relevant messages in the archive, and 3 of them are in the top 10. What is recall at 10?
questions.explanation: Recall at 10 divides the relevant messages found (3) by the relevant messages a list of ten could hold, min(10, 6) = 6: 0.50.
misconceptions: Divides by the length of the list: that is precision at 10
Divides the relevant messages by the list length
Counts a query as solved when any relevant message appears

questions.prompt: A character n-gram search scores recall at 10 of 0.45 for English queries and 0.03 for queries written in Arabizi. The relevant messages for each query are in all four varieties. What explains the Arabizi number best?
options: The metric divides by the wrong number of relevant messages for this variety
Arabizi queries are shorter than English queries
The index holds fewer Arabizi messages than it should
Arabizi spellings vary, so few letter sequences are shared
questions.explanation: A lexical search finds shared letter sequences; Arabizi has no fixed spelling, so a query shares few of them even with other Arabizi messages, and none with Arabic script.
misconceptions: Suspects the metric although the same code scored English
Blames length: the queries are of similar length in every variety
Suspects the index when the baseline simply cannot match across spellings

questions.prompt: Agents search the archive two ways: by a description of the problem, and by a ticket number such as SW-48213. The vector search is good at the first and poor at the second. What should the team build?
options: An exact lookup for ticket numbers beside it
A second vector index that holds only ticket numbers
A rule that rewrites ticket numbers into words before embedding
A larger embedding model for both kinds of query
questions.explanation: A ticket number has no meaning to embed; exact identifiers need exact matching, and the two searches can sit side by side.
misconceptions: Keeps the wrong tool for the job in a second copy
Invents a transformation that adds no meaning
Expects size to give meaning to an identifier

questions.prompt: A grounded assistant answers 20 questions from a rule book. For 5 wrong answers, the rule that answers the question was not among the retrieved chunks. For 2 others, the rule was retrieved and the reply states a wrong figure. Which part needs work first?
options: The evaluation set, because seven errors in twenty are too many to be real
The generator, because it wrote all seven wrong answers
The retriever, because five errors happen before the model reads
The prompt, because a stricter prompt fixes both kinds
questions.explanation: In five cases the model never saw the rule, so no prompt can fix them; the retriever is the larger and earlier cause.
misconceptions: Dismisses the measurement instead of reading it
Attributes every error to the last step of the pipeline
Expects a prompt to supply a rule that is not in the context

questions.prompt: A grounded assistant must tell the customer when the rule book does not answer a question. Why does the course ask for the exact reply NOT_IN_RULES and not a polite sentence?
options: A fixed string is cheaper to generate than a sentence
Code can detect it, count it and hand the question on
Customers prefer short replies to long ones
The model cannot write polite sentences when the temperature is 0
questions.explanation: An exact string can be tested and acted on by code; a free sentence that means the same cannot be counted reliably.
misconceptions: Thinks of token cost, which is negligible here
Confuses the internal signal with the text a customer finally sees
Misreads what temperature does

questions.prompt: An extractor is scored on 100 messages for the field district. The gold data has a district in 60 messages. The extractor returns a district in 50 messages, and 45 of those are right. What are precision and recall for this field?
options: Precision 0.45, recall 0.75
Precision 0.75, recall 0.90
Precision 0.90, recall 0.45
Precision 0.90, recall 0.75
questions.explanation: Precision is right values over returned values, 45 / 50 = 0.90; recall is right values over gold values, 45 / 60 = 0.75.
misconceptions: Divides the right values by all 100 messages for precision
Swaps the two definitions
Divides the right values by all 100 messages for recall

questions.prompt: Before a message goes to a hosted model, the account number is replaced by [ACCOUNT_1]. The model returns the account field as 3055512345. The message had no such number. What should the service do?
options: Reject it, because the model only saw a placeholder
Accept it when the number exists in the customer table
Reject it only when the confidence is low
Accept it, because it matches the pattern of an account number
questions.explanation: The model saw masked text, so a real-looking number in its answer cannot come from the message: it is invented, and the validator rejects it.
misconceptions: Lets an invented value pass because it happens to exist
Waits for a confidence that an extraction reply does not carry
Checks the shape of the value and not where it came from

questions.prompt: A masking step replaces phone numbers that match 05 and eight digits. Its test passes on 200 messages. In production, a customer writes the phone number as ٠٥٥ ١٢٣ ٤٥٦٧ and it reaches the hosted model. Which two things did the masking miss?
options: A wrong country code and a missing name
Diacritics on the digits and a long message
A second phone number and a greeting in English
Arabic-Indic digits, and spaces in the number
questions.explanation: The pattern expects ten Western digits in a row; this number is in Arabic-Indic digits and is broken by spaces, so the pattern never matches.
misconceptions: Looks for causes that are not in the example
Applies letter problems to digits
Invents content the message does not have

questions.prompt: An extraction reply fails validation, is repaired once, and fails again. The course's loop then logs the failure and returns no fields. Why does it not try a third and fourth time?
options: A third reply would overwrite the log entry of the first
Validation errors are random, so further retries could make no difference
Each retry costs a call and rarely succeeds after two failures
The provider forbids more than two calls for one message
questions.explanation: Retries have a price and falling returns; a logged failure goes to a person, which is safer than a guessed value.
misconceptions: Misunderstands the log, which keeps one entry per attempt
Treats systematic errors as chance
Invents a provider rule

questions.prompt: A linear layer has a weight matrix of 512 by 512. You add a low-rank adapter of rank 4 to it. How many trainable numbers does the adapter have?
misconceptions: Counts only one of the two matrices
Doubles the rank or counts each matrix twice
Counts the frozen weight matrix itself

questions.prompt: A model has 100 million parameters. With Adam, a trainable weight needs 16 bytes during training and a frozen 32-bit weight needs 4 bytes. You train adapters that are 1% of the parameters and freeze the rest. About how much memory do the weights need during training?
options: 0.4 GB
0.6 GB
1.6 GB
2.0 GB
questions.explanation: Frozen: 99 million × 4 bytes = 396 MB. Trainable: 1 million × 16 bytes = 16 MB. Together about 412 MB, or 0.4 GB.
misconceptions: Adds a full copy of gradients for the frozen weights
Charges every weight as trainable
Charges every weight as trainable and adds the frozen copy again

questions.prompt: On the same split, full fine-tuning of a small encoder reaches test macro F1 0.63 with 530,000 trainable parameters. A rank-8 adapter reaches 0.41 with 9,000. Training memory is not a constraint for this model. Which run do you carry into the comparison with the baseline?
options: The adapter, because a model with fewer trainable parameters always generalises better
The full run, because memory is not scarce and it scores higher
Neither, because the two runs cannot be compared
The adapter, because it trains 98% fewer parameters
questions.explanation: An adapter trades quality for memory; when memory is not scarce, the saving buys nothing and the higher score decides.
misconceptions: Turns a tendency into a rule that the measured scores contradict
Refuses a comparison made on the same split with the same metric
Optimises a number that is not the constraint

questions.prompt: A routing model scores macro F1 0.91 on a random split and 0.86 when the split keeps each customer on one side. A third of the customers wrote the same complaint more than once. Which number predicts the score on a customer who has never written before?
options: The mean of the two, 0.885
Neither, because both numbers were measured on the same data
0.91, because it uses more varied training data
0.86, because no copy of a test message was trained on
questions.explanation: With a random split, near-copies of test messages sit in the training set, so the test is partly a memory test; the split by customer removes that.
misconceptions: Averages a biased and an unbiased estimate
Overlooks that the way of splitting is exactly what differs
Mistakes leakage for variety

questions.prompt: A colleague fine-tunes with six learning rates, scores each run on the test split, and reports the best test score as the model's quality. What is the flaw?
options: The test split chose the learning rate, so it is no longer unseen
The learning rate should be chosen on the training loss
The best score should be averaged with the worst
Six runs are too few to find a good learning rate for an encoder of this size
questions.explanation: Choosing among runs by test score fits the choice to the test split; a validation split is for choosing, the test split for one final measurement.
misconceptions: Chooses on the data the model has memorised
Proposes arithmetic that does not remove the selection effect
Focuses on the size of the search and misses the leak

questions.prompt: A router for three departments has F1 of 0.90 for billing (500 test messages), 0.80 for supply (400) and 0.10 for connections (100). What is its macro F1?
questions.explanation: Macro F1 is the plain mean over departments: (0.90 + 0.80 + 0.10) / 3 = 0.60.
misconceptions: Rounds a size-weighted mean downwards
Weights each department by its number of messages
Reports the best department

questions.prompt: Three routers are measured on the same test split. A: macro F1 0.85, Arabizi 0.42, 5 ms at the 95th percentile, no cost per call. B: 0.88, Arabizi 0.70, 900 ms, 0.04 USD per 1,000. C: 0.63, Arabizi 0.28, 20 ms, no cost per call. The budget is 300 ms at the 95th percentile. Which recommendation holds?
options: A for all messages, and nothing more to do
A, with Arabizi handed to a person or sent to B off the real-time path
B for all messages, because it has the highest macro F1
C for all messages, because a neural model will improve as more data arrives
questions.explanation: B breaks the latency budget and C is worse than A everywhere; A fits the budget, and its weak variety needs a hand-off or a slower path.
misconceptions: Accepts 0.42 for one customer group without a rule for it
Ignores the latency budget
Chooses on a hope instead of the measurements

questions.prompt: On 40 test messages, ten per variety, model X scores 0.70 for Gulf and model Y scores 0.60. On 400 messages, 150 of them Gulf, the two models score 0.82 and 0.84 for Gulf. What should you conclude?
options: X is better for Gulf, as the first test showed
Y is better for Gulf, as the second test showed
The two are close for Gulf; ten messages cannot rank them
The second test is wrong, because both scores changed between the tests
questions.explanation: With ten messages one error moves the score by several points; on 150 messages the models are two points apart, which is still within noise.
misconceptions: Trusts the smaller sample
Reads a two-point gap as a ranking
Expects scores to be stable across sample sizes

questions.prompt: A prompted router gives the same message two different departments on two runs. The team sets the temperature to 0 and the label is now stable. What do they know about the label?
options: It is stable; whether it is right is unmeasured
It is correct, because the model is now certain
It is the label most customers would choose
It will stay the same after a change to another model
questions.explanation: Temperature 0 removes the random draw; the single remaining answer is the model's most likely one, right or wrong.
misconceptions: Confuses repeatability with correctness
Reads a model probability as a survey
Extends a setting's effect to another model

questions.prompt: A routing service passes its smoke test: 24 messages, all answered with status 200, and the four edge cases handed to a person. What does this result establish?
options: The service routes at least 20 of 24 messages correctly
The model's macro F1 is above the hand-off threshold
The service meets its latency budget at the 95th percentile
The service answers and handles the edge cases
questions.explanation: A smoke test checks that the service answers and handles edge cases; quality needs the held-out test split, and latency its own measurement.
misconceptions: Reads correctness into a test that did not check labels
Mixes a score with a threshold
Assumes a timing that the test did not take

questions.prompt: A model card reports macro F1 0.85 on the test split and says the model supports Arabic and English. By variety the scores are MSA 0.94, Gulf 0.86, English 0.81 and Arabizi 0.42. Which line must be added before the card is signed?
options: The average length of a message in tokens
The number of parameters of the model
Results by variety and a hand-off rule for Arabizi
The name of the engineer who trained and evaluated the model
questions.explanation: A card states limits by subgroup: one customer group is served far worse than the average says, and the card must say when its messages go to a person.
misconceptions: Adds a statistic that does not show the failure
Adds a fact that changes no decision
Adds provenance where the missing part is a limit

questions.prompt: A service hands a message to a person when the best probability is below 0.5, or 0.7 for Arabizi. An Arabizi message gets leaks with probability 0.62 and an English message gets billing with 0.55. What happens to the two messages?
options: Both are handed to a person
The Arabizi one goes to a person; the English one is routed
The English message is handed to a person; the Arabizi one is routed
Both are routed by the model
questions.explanation: 0.62 is below the Arabizi threshold of 0.7, so that message is handed off; 0.55 is above the general threshold of 0.5, so the English one is routed.
misconceptions: Applies the Arabizi threshold to both
Swaps the two thresholds
Applies the general threshold to both

questions.prompt: A model answers in 4 ms when called in a notebook. Behind the service, the same message takes 9 ms at the median and 35 ms at the 95th percentile. The budget is 300 ms at the 95th percentile. What do you report?
options: 35 ms, a breach because it is eight times the model's latency
The mean of 9 ms and 35 ms
4 ms, the model's own latency
9 ms and 35 ms through the service, inside the budget
questions.explanation: The customer waits for the service, not for the model alone; the median and the 95th percentile through the service are the numbers to report against the budget.
misconceptions: Compares with the wrong reference: the budget is 300 ms
Averages two percentiles into a number with no meaning
Reports the part instead of the whole path
